step_1: The current environment is a stationary Wi-Fi (802.11g) setup using the Reno congestion control algorithm. The application is video streaming, which is currently experiencing high RTT (136ms) and insufficient throughput (8.17 Mbps), leading to a poor QoE score of 0.63.
step_2: Key metrics from the IFA report show an average RTT of 136.55 ms (exceeding the 90ms target), throughput of 8.17 Mbps (below the 12 Mbps target), and significant packet loss (mean 244.61 segments). The CWND is fluctuating significantly (σ=25.15).
step_3: The target QoS profile requires E2e delay ≤ 90 ms and throughput ≥ 12 Mbps. Currently, neither is met, resulting in pixelated video and choppy visual quality.
step_4: Reno's behavior of halving the CWND (Multiplicative Decrease) upon any loss is detrimental in this Wi-Fi environment, where non-congestive (random) wireless losses are likely. This causes the throughput to stay below the required threshold for stable 720p/1080p streaming.
step_5: The current control logic is too sensitive to loss. It lacks a mechanism to distinguish between congestion and wireless noise, and its recovery is too slow for high-bandwidth video requirements.
step_6: I will adjust the ssthresh calculation to reduce the CWND by only 30% (keeping 70%) instead of 50% upon loss. This 'gentler' reduction will help maintain higher average throughput on the lossy 802.11g link.
step_7: By maintaining a larger CWND after loss events, the algorithm will recover to the target 12 Mbps throughput faster, reducing buffering events and improving the visual quality of the video stream.
step_8: Action: Generate a new congestion control algorithm (llm_cc_3_1) with a modified ssthresh (0.7 multiplier) to better handle Wi-Fi signal fluctuations and meet video streaming demands.
